title: Tazria: after a birth (Leviticus 12)
hook: a new mother's time apart and her offering mark a life-changing passage

segments.voice: Yesterday, kadosh: holy, set apart, right down to the dinner plate. Your line was holy in the everyday. Today, a new portion, and a new life.

Ask anyone who has just had a baby how they are, and watch their face try to answer. Exhausted. Overjoyed. Sore. Terrified. Sometimes all four before lunch. Outside, the world goes on as usual; inside the house, everything has moved. The next portion of Leviticus is called Tazria, from its opening verb: when a woman conceives. And before it turns to skin and sickness, it stops for one short chapter, only eight verses, to mark what happens to a woman after she gives birth.
screen: `EXHAUSTED, OVERJOYED, SORE.` → `EVERYTHING HAS MOVED.` → `TAZRIA: WHEN A WOMAN CONCEIVES.`

segments.voice: Start with the time apart. After a birth, the mother enters a period of ritual impurity, called tumah, and then days of purification: for a boy, seven days and then thirty-three; for a girl, fourteen and then sixty-six. The Torah gives the numbers and not the reasons, and nobody knows for certain why they differ. Tumah isn't dirt, and it isn't sin. In Leviticus it comes from contact with the edges of life: birth, death, bodily flows. A priest burying his own parent becomes impure too. Some teachers read the mother's time apart as a recognition that she has just been to the very edge of life and back. In practice, it meant weeks when she didn't come to the sanctuary, and wasn't expected to. When the days are full, she brings a lamb and a dove or pigeon. And then a line that matters: if she can't afford a lamb, two birds will do. Nobody is priced out of marking a birth. The Talmud asks why a mother brings a sin offering at all, and one answer is gentle: in the pain of labor, a woman may swear things she never means to keep. Birth changes the mother, not only the household. Leviticus gives that change a time, a boundary and a ceremony, so it isn't just swallowed by the week. Today, Jewish communities mark births with a bris for boys, naming ceremonies for girls, and a blessing of thanks a mother can say in synagogue.
screen: `DAYS APART, BY THE CALENDAR.` · `TUMAH: NOT DIRT, NOT SIN.` · `A LAMB, OR TWO BIRDS.` · `A PASSAGE WITH A BOUNDARY.` · then, large: `BIRTH CHANGES EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has recently had a baby, or adopted one, or is about to, or your own parents the year you arrived. Think about what that season actually asked of them: the nights, the body, the fear, the joy. If you pray, remember them in your prayers; if not, simply hold them in mind for a while.
Tazria. When a woman conceives: the portion that opens by marking a mother's passage after birth, with time apart and an offering anyone can afford.
Your line: birth changes everything. A new parent is someone new, too. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Jewish communities mark a birth with a brit milah for a boy on the eighth day and a naming for a girl, often at the Torah reading or a simchat bat; in many communities a mother says Birkat Hagomel, the blessing of thanks after danger, when she returns to synagogue.

chat.says: Leviticus calls a new mother impure. Does that mean birth is sinful or dirty?
options: No. In Leviticus, tumah isn't dirt or sin; it comes from touching the edges of life.
No, but it means the baby is impure, so the father must keep the newborn apart.
No, it only applies when the birth happens on Shabbat or a festival day.
chat.meaning: Tumah isn't dirt and isn't sin. In Leviticus it comes from contact with the edges of life, like birth and death; even a priest burying a parent becomes impure.

notes: Numbers checked against Lev 12: boy 7 + 33 days, girl 14 + 66; offering a lamb and a pigeon or turtledove; two birds if she cannot afford a lamb (12:8).
